newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's San Paolo clears decks for privatisation.
newsitem.headline: Italy's San Paolo clears decks for privatisation.

text.p: Italy's largest commercial bank Istituto Bancario San Paolo di Torino, currently owned by a public foundation, will be taken into private hands by mid-1997, San Paolo chairman Gianni Zandano said on Monday.

Zandano told a news conference in Turin that the bank intended to complete a process of privatisation, initiated in 1992 with a listing on the stock exchange, by making a placement of around 20 percent of San Paolo's stock by the end of April.
The private placement with a stable core of Italian and overseas shareholders would be a prelude to a public offering of around 25 percent of the bank's capital to domestic and foreign investors.

"We have a deadline which is partly due to the need to base the prospectus on up-to-date figures and we cannot go much beyond the first six months," said Zandano. "We hope if possible to complete (the privatisation) during the first half.
None of the stable core of shareholders would own more than five percent of the bank, giving no single owner a pre-eminent position.

Zandano, who opposes the shareholder syndicates which have been a hall-mark of Italy's closely-knit business establishment, said he wanted a looser arrangement among core shareholders giving a bigger role to small investors and making the bank at least theoretically vulnerable to hostile takeover.
"We think the Italian market is mature and we are aiming to create a public company," Zandano said.

San Paolo's dominant shareholder, San Paolo Holding, with a 65.58 percent stake in the bank, will see its stake fall to no more than 20 to 25 percent after the privatisation, Zandano said. San Paolo Holding is in turn wholly owned by Compagnia di San Paolo, a public foundation.

Asked what would become of the Holding after the privatisation, Zandano said the decision ultimately lay with the Compagnia. "Only the Compagnia can decide whether to suppress the Holding or it could even decide to merge it with another bank," he added.

Other major shareholders in the bank include the Italian treasury, with 3.36 percent, Spain's Banco Santander with three percent and Italian investment bank Istituto Mobiliare Italiano (IMI) with 1.82 percent.
Zandano said he hoped both banks could be persuaded to exercise an option to raise their respective shareholdings to five percent each.
He was also hoping to woo Turin-based auto group Fiat and investors from France, Germany and possibly Britain into subscribing to the private placement.

"I personally hope that the most important productive force in Turin is present in the shareholding structure," he said. Zandano also denied news reports that U.S. industrial group General Electric had been asked to become a core shareholder.
He added: "My hope is that also France, Germany and maybe even Britain can be present in our shareholding. I say this on the basis of facts that I cannot divulge."

Zandano also anounced that San Paolo had made a consolidated net profit of 600 billion lire in 1996, an increase of 36 percent on the previous year. The bank said it would pay a dividend of 280 lire, up from 240 lire the previous year.

In a separate development San Paolo announced that Franco-Belgian bank Dexia, which finances public works and local authorities, would take a 40 percent stake in Crediop, a wholly-owned San Paolo subsidiary operating in the same sector, as part of a long-term strategic alliance.
The Crediop stake would be valued at between 480 and 565 billion lire although the final worth of the deal would be determined by Crediop's profits record in the coming three years.

Dexia, established in 1996 through a linkup between Credit Local de France and Credit Communal de Belgique, said from Paris that it also wanted a one percent stake in San Paolo when the Italian bank is privatised. $=1,658
